Newborn Care

The First 24 Hours With a Newborn: What to Expect

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

In the first 24 hours with a newborn, expect an alert hour or two of skin to skin contact and a first feed, then long sleepy stretches, routine checks and medicines, about one wet diaper, a first black tarry stool, and often a much more wakeful second night. Hospitals add a few standard steps on the birth day, like the vitamin K injection and hearing screen, and most now wait at least a day before the first bath. This guide walks through the day roughly in order, so you can read it from a hospital bed one section at a time.

The golden hour: skin to skin and the first feed

Right after birth, most healthy babies can go straight onto your bare chest. A nurse or midwife dries the baby, covers you both with a warm blanket, and often adds a little hat. This is the golden hour: roughly the first 60 to 90 minutes, kept quiet and unhurried. Skin to skin contact helps a newborn's temperature, breathing, heart rate, and blood sugar settle, and it calms both of you. Many routine checks, including the quick Apgar assessments at one and five minutes, can happen while the baby stays on you. If you have a cesarean birth or your baby needs extra help breathing, skin to skin can start as soon as it is safe, and a partner can hold the baby against their chest in the meantime.

Most babies are surprisingly alert in that first hour or two, and many start rooting, licking, and searching for the breast on their own. The World Health Organization and other major health bodies encourage a first breastfeed within the first hour when possible. Do not worry about volume. Your early milk, colostrum, comes in small amounts that match a stomach the size of a marble, and it is rich in protective factors. Ask your nurse, midwife, or a lactation consultant to sit with you for that first feed; hands-on help now prevents problems later. If you are formula feeding, the first small bottle usually happens in the same window. Positioning and latch details have their own guide, so for now, just get help early.

Routine medicines on the birth day, in plain language

Within the first hours, your baby will be weighed, measured, and offered two routine treatments. The first is a vitamin K injection, usually given in the thigh. Newborns are born with very little vitamin K, and the injection prevents a rare but serious bleeding problem called vitamin K deficiency bleeding. The second, routine in most United States hospitals, is erythromycin eye ointment, a thin antibiotic strip that protects against certain eye infections picked up during birth; practice varies in other countries, so ask what your hospital does. Both can typically wait until after the first feed and can often be done while your baby lies on your chest. Ask the staff to walk you through anything before it happens; that is a normal request, not a difficult one.

Your baby will also be offered a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine, recommended within 24 hours of birth in the United States. It protects against a virus that can quietly damage the liver over a lifetime, and giving it early works well. Expect frequent visits from the care team during the first day: temperature checks, heart rate, breathing, color, and blood sugar checks for some babies, such as those born early, small, large, or to a parent with diabetes. It can feel like a lot of interruptions. Each check has a purpose, and you can always ask what the team is looking for and what the results mean.

Screening tests and the delayed first bath

Two screening tests usually happen before you go home. The newborn blood spot test, often called the heel prick, takes a few drops of blood from the heel, typically after 24 hours of age. It screens for a set of rare but treatable conditions, and finding them early can prevent serious harm. The hearing screen is painless and is often done while your baby sleeps; a small earpiece plays soft sounds and measures the response. Neither test needs you to leave your baby. You can hold or feed your baby during the heel prick, which genuinely helps with comfort. If a screen needs repeating, that is common and usually not a sign something is wrong.

Many hospitals now wait at least 24 hours before the first bath, in line with World Health Organization guidance. A newborn arrives coated in vernix, the white creamy layer that protected the skin in the womb. Leaving it on helps the skin, and delaying the bath helps babies hold their temperature and blood sugar steady and settle into feeding. Staff will still wipe away blood and fluid soon after birth. When bath time comes, you can usually watch or do it yourself with a nurse coaching you, which is a good confidence builder before you go home. If your family has a tradition around early bathing, tell the team; timing can often be discussed.

Sleep, feeds, and diapers on day one

After that alert first stretch, most newborns fall into a deep recovery sleep that can last several hours, and then doze on and off for much of the day. Sleeping 16 hours or more across the first 24 hours is typical. Feeds are small and frequent once the baby wakes, often 8 to 12 times in 24 hours over the first days. In the beginning, many care teams suggest waking a sleepy baby to feed if more than about three to four hours have passed. Jot feed times, wet diapers, and questions somewhere easy, on paper or in the BeMama app, because the first day blurs quickly and the numbers help at checkups.

Diaper expectations on day one are modest. Roughly one wet diaper in the first 24 hours is normal, and most babies pass their first stool, a black sticky tar called meconium, within the first day or so. Counts climb steadily after that, and the day by day numbers are covered in our diaper output guide. Weight comes up at nearly every check because newborns normally lose some at first, often up to about 7 to 10 percent of birth weight, before regaining it by around two weeks. A loss inside that range with good feeding is expected, not a failure. The team will tell you if the trend needs a closer look.

The second night, and when to ask for help

Many parents are surprised by the second night. After a sleepy first day, babies often wake up to the world around 24 hours old and want to feed constantly, cry when put down, and settle only on a warm chest. This is common newborn behavior, not proof that your milk is not enough; frequent feeding at this stage actually helps your supply come in. Keep the baby close, feed on cues, and trade off with a partner so each of you gets a stretch of rest. If you are exhausted and starting to doze while holding the baby, put the baby in the bassinet or press the call button. Falling asleep together in a hospital bed or chair is a real risk, and staff would much rather help.

Some things on the birth day deserve a prompt call to your nurse, midwife, or clinician rather than watchful waiting. Tell someone right away if your baby's skin or eyes look yellow within the first 24 hours, since early jaundice needs prompt evaluation. The same goes for fast or labored breathing, grunting, blue lips or tongue, a baby who feels hot or unusually cold, a baby too sleepy to wake for any feeds, or no wet diaper by 24 hours. If you have already gone home and your baby has blue lips, is struggling to breathe, or cannot be woken, call emergency services right away rather than waiting for a callback. Speak up about your own body too: soaking a pad in an hour, severe headache, chest pain, trouble breathing, or feeling suddenly unwell all need immediate attention, by call button in the hospital or emergency services at home. This is exactly what the team is there for.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Newborn care centres on frequent responsive feeding, safe sleep, warmth without overheating, hygiene, and timely follow-up. Clinicians assess the whole picture: including alertness, feeding effectiveness, growth, urine and stool output, colour, and breathing.

A young baby can become unwell quickly, so caregiver concern and sudden change matter. Routine records help describe what happened but cannot determine whether a newborn is medically well.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to coordinate feeding, diapers, sleep, temperature, appointments, and which caregiver recorded each event. Do not delay care to complete a log.

When to seek help

Seek prompt professional advice for poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, repeated vomiting, dehydration concerns, or any temperature concern in a young baby.

Sources and further reading

  • Public Health Agency of Canada — Safe Sleep for Your Baby
  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Fever and Your Baby

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Skin to skin contact and a first feed within the first hour help a newborn stabilize and start feeding well.
  • Vitamin K, erythromycin eye ointment, and a first hepatitis B vaccine are routine on the birth day.
  • Many hospitals wait at least 24 hours before the first bath to protect temperature, blood sugar, and feeding.
  • Expect about one wet diaper, a first meconium stool, and 16 or more hours of sleep on day one.
  • A wakeful second night is normal, but early jaundice, breathing trouble, or no wet diaper by 24 hours needs prompt attention.

Frequently asked questions

What is the golden hour after birth?

The golden hour is the first hour or so after birth, spent with your baby skin to skin on your chest while routine tasks are kept to a minimum. It helps a newborn's temperature, breathing, and blood sugar settle and gives the first feed a natural starting point. If a cesarean birth or medical care delays it, skin to skin still helps whenever it starts.

How soon after birth should a baby breastfeed?

Within the first hour when possible, which is the standard recommendation from the World Health Organization and other major health bodies. Most babies are alert and ready to try during that window. If the first feed is delayed for medical reasons, ask staff to help you start as soon as your baby is able and to show you hand expression in the meantime.

When do newborns get their first bath?

Most hospitals now wait at least 24 hours after birth before the first bath, in line with World Health Organization guidance. Delaying protects the baby's temperature and blood sugar, supports early feeding, and leaves the protective vernix coating on the skin. Blood and fluid are wiped away soon after birth either way.

How much do newborns sleep on the first day?

Most newborns sleep about 16 hours or more in the first 24 hours, starting with a deep recovery sleep of several hours after an alert first hour or two, then dozing on and off. Feeds still need to happen, so care teams often suggest waking a baby who sleeps more than about three to four hours in these first days. Expect the second night to be far more wakeful.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
